Show that the out-shuffle sends the card in position $i$ to position $2i\bmod 51$ for $i\le50$, and fixes position $51$; then show that $8$ out-shuffles restore the deck. How many in-shuffles are needed? (Use Volume~2.)

entries.context: Write $\Q(\zeta)$ for the smallest subfield of $\C$ containing $\Q$ and $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/p}$. Here $\Phi_p(X)=1+X+\cdots+X^{p-1}$, so $(X-1)\Phi_p(X)=X^p-1$. The exercise on Eisenstein's criterion in Volume~1's polynomial chapter proves that $\Phi_p$ is irreducible over $\Q$: after the shift $X\mapsto X+1$ it is Eisenstein at $p$. If $P(\zeta)=0$, division by $\Phi_p$ leaves a remainder $R$ of degree less than $p-1$. A nonzero such $R$ would be coprime to $\Phi_p$ by irreducibility; the polynomial B\'ezout identity would evaluate to $1=0$ at $\zeta$. Thus $\Phi_p$ divides $P$.

entries.context: Taking norms in $(a+bi+cj+dk)(a'+b'i+c'j+d'k)$ gives Euler's four-square identity (Exercise~\ref{ex:euler4}), used in Volume~2 to reduce the four-square theorem to primes. A classification result beyond our proofs is Frobenius's theorem: $\R$, $\C$ and $\mathbb H$ are the only finite-dimensional associative division algebras over $\R$. Dropping associativity alone does not give a comparable list. For nonzero finite-dimensional real algebras with an identity and a squared Euclidean length satisfying $N(xy)=N(x)N(y)$, Hurwitz's theorem gives $\R$, $\C$, $\mathbb H$ and the eight-dimensional octonions. Neither classification is a premise below.
